analysis.one_liner: Caps malpractice payouts for injured obstetric and gynecological patients at $250,000 for pain and suffering.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on February 10, 2005 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for lawsuits over negligent obstetric and gynecological care. It capped compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000, shortened the deadlines for filing a claim, cut the contingency fees plaintiffs' lawyers could collect, reduced awards by any insurance or benefits the patient had already received, made punitive damages nearly impossible to win, and barred naming a health care provider in a product-liability suit over an FDA-approved drug or device. Supporters framed it as a way to lower malpractice insurance costs and keep doctors delivering babies; its actual terms all reduced what injured patients could recover.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors who deliver obstetric and gynecological care, hospitals, medical malpractice insurers, and drug and device makers would gain the most, because every provision lowers the maximum they could be made to pay a patient harmed by negligent care. Malpractice insurers benefit directly from the damage caps; providers benefit from shorter filing deadlines, weaker punitive damages, and the shield from product-liability suits over FDA-approved drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Malpractice insurers, OB-GYNs, and drug makers

how_it_helps.text: Caps noneconomic damages — pain, suffering, disfigurement, loss of companionship — at $250,000 no matter how many defendants or claims are involved, while leaving economic losses like medical bills and lost earnings uncapped.

Cuts every claim's award by any collateral source benefits the patient is entitled to — health insurance, disability, workers' compensation — unless that payor has a legal right to reimbursement, which effectively makes patients pay twice for harms their own insurance already covered.

Allows punitive damages only on clear and convincing evidence of malicious intent to injure or deliberate failure to avoid certain injury, caps them at the greater of twice economic damages or $250,000, and does not tell the jury the cap exists.
Sets a filing deadline of three years after the injury shows itself or one year after discovery, and caps plaintiffs' lawyers' contingency fees on a sliding scale from 40% down to 15%.
Prohibits naming a health care provider as a defendant in a product-liability or class-action suit for prescribing or dispensing an FDA-approved drug or device.

analysis.who_pays: Patients harmed by negligent obstetric or gynecological care, especially families of babies with birth injuries whose largest losses are pain and suffering rather than measurable bills. Plaintiffs' medical-malpractice attorneys also bear the cost through fee caps. Nothing in the bill guarantees premiums would fall or that more doctors would offer obstetric care.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients injured by negligent OB-GYN care

drawbacks.text: A $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages would fall hardest on the worst cases, such as a baby with a lifelong birth injury, whose damages are mostly noneconomic; economic losses like care bills remain uncapped, but the cap removes most of the jury's ability to value the injury itself.

Reducing awards by collateral source benefits means a patient who paid premiums for health or disability coverage can recover less because that coverage paid out, shifting the loss back onto the injured family.

Requiring clear and convincing proof of malicious intent before punitive damages can even be sought makes punishment effectively unavailable for negligent conduct that falls short of intent to injure, and the bill requires a court finding before a punitive claim may even be added to a lawsuit.

A one-year clock from discovery and a three-year overall limit could bar claims by patients who learn of the injury late, subject only to narrow exceptions for fraud, concealment, or a left-behind foreign object.

Supporters' premise — that these limits would lower malpractice premiums and improve access to obstetric care — is an assumption the bill does not guarantee or enforce; the savings would flow first to insurers and providers regardless.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — keeping obstetric care available by lowering malpractice costs — rests on the theory that capping lawsuits lowers premiums and retains doctors. The bill itself contains no mechanism requiring insurers to pass savings along or guaranteeing access to care, so the certain effect would have been smaller recoveries for the relatively few families with the worst injuries, with any premium relief indirect and unguaranteed. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the tradeoff falls entirely on patients who were already harmed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee in February 2005, and no one ever gave it a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Judd Gregg, joined by Sen. John Ensign, introduced the bill in the Senate on February 10, 2005.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill's complete action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call at any point before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

Had it become law, it would have capped noneconomic damages in obstetric and gynecological malpractice cases at $250,000 and made a series of other changes reducing what injured patients could recover.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients injured by negligent obstetric or gynecological care kept the full remedies available under existing state law, including uncapped state awards where allowed. Because the bill never moved, no one gained the liability relief it promised; insurers and providers simply remained under the pre-existing rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients kept existing malpractice rights

for.name: Sen. Judd Gregg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Sen. John Ensign
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill with Sen. Gregg.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or a markup on the bill after its referral on February 10, 2005.

sides.party_line_note: All four senators publicly attached to the bill — the sponsor and three cosponsors — were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it, and no vote was ever taken to test broader support.

industries.note: Damage caps, the collateral-source offset, and near-elimination of punitive damages would all directly reduce what the insurer pays a patient harmed by negligent care. Supporters argued lower payouts would lower premiums, but the bill required no insurer to pass savings along.

Providers would face shorter filing deadlines, weaker punitive exposure, capped patient awards, and a shield from product-liability suits over FDA-approved drugs they prescribe. Supporters argued this relief protects patients' access to care by keeping doctors in practice, but the direct financial effect is paying injured patients less.

The bill's caps and punitive-damages limits apply to manufacturers and sellers of medical products used in obstetric or gynecological care, and it bars naming providers in product-liability suits, narrowing the paths a harmed patient could use against the drug or device itself.

Sliding-scale caps on contingency fees and shorter, harder filing deadlines would cut both the income and the caseload of lawyers who represent injured patients. Their interest in this bill ran with their clients' recovery.
